Canada has introduced tougher penalties for immigration consultants and other representatives who provide unauthorized immigration services or deliberately submit false information on behalf of applicants, with fines reaching up to $1.07 million. The new regulations are part of the Canadian government’s efforts to protect foreign nationals from immigration fraud, prevent exploitation and strengthen accountability among individuals offering paid immigration and citizenship services. According to a post obtained from the Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC’s) website on Friday, the rules apply to both licensed and unlicensed representatives, including individuals operating outside Canada. The development could affect immigration agents serving Nigerian applicants seeking Canadian study permits, work permits and permanent residency, as the regulations cover paid immigration services regardless of where the representative operates. Under the new framework, individuals found providing paid immigration or citizenship advice without proper authorization could face penalties starting at CAD5,000. Those who knowingly provide false or misleading information on behalf of applicants, or assist in submitting such information, could face fines of CAD15,000. Additional penalties may apply where an immigration application is approved based on inaccurate information, while repeat violations could attract cumulative fines of up to CAD1.5 million, depending on the seriousness and frequency of the offences. The Immigration Minister, Lena Metlege Diab, said the measures were designed to ensure that people seeking to build a future in Canada receive reliable immigration advice. The government said the penalties would apply to paid representatives, including licensed immigration consultants, lawyers and other authorized professionals, as well as individuals providing such services without authorization. The regulations also apply to representatives operating outside Canada, meaning immigration agents based in Nigeria and other countries could face penalties if they violate the rules while providing paid services to applicants. The online registry is expected to become operational in 2027, following the issuance of the first penalties. According to the Canadian government, the registry will enable prospective applicants to identify representatives who have previously been penalized for misconduct. The measures also introduce stronger inspection powers, allowing authorities to examine records and request documents from individuals offering paid immigration and citizenship services. Representatives who receive a notice of violation will have 30 days to pay the penalty or request a formal review. Nigerian applicants urged to verify immigration agents The new regulations reinforce the need for Nigerians seeking Canadian visas and permanent residency to verify the credentials of immigration representatives before paying for their services. Paid immigration consultants must be licensed by the College of Immigration and Citizenship Consultants (CICC), while lawyers must belong to the relevant Canadian law society. Notaries in Quebec may also provide authorized immigration services. IRCC has also warned that applicants remain responsible for the accuracy of information submitted on their behalf, even when they use an immigration representative. According to the department, submitting false information or documents could result in an application refusal and a ban from entering Canada for at least five years. The government has therefore advised applicants to provide accurate personal, educational, employment and financial information throughout the immigration process. The latest regulations build on Canada’s broader efforts to combat immigration fraud, strengthen oversight of immigration representatives and protect foreign nationals from exploitation.
